newsitem.title: USA: Space shuttle slips into a publicity black hole.
newsitem.headline: Space shuttle slips into a publicity black hole.

text.p: Outshone by Pathfinder's spectacular vistas of Mars and an unfolding drama aboard Russia's Mir space station, the U.S. space shuttle Columbia seems to have slipped into a publicity black hole.

Its 16-day science mission, which blasted off on July 1, has come nowhere near the excitement of the Mars Pathfinder landing or the nail-biting tension of the fight for survival by three spacemen aboard the crippled Mir space station.

The shuttle's 33 scientific experiments have worthy goals, but explaining them to the public is not always easy, NASA spokesman Dave Drachlis said. "It's pretty difficult to talk about the individual experiments but I think that message is getting out that our microgravity research programme is designed to improve life on Earth," he said.

The Mars landing and drama on Mir may in fact have boosted interest in the mission, he gamely added. "It's a great week for NASA and the space programme in general. It's essentially a three-part story."

NASA's shuttle mission Web site on the Internet has received about three million "hits" since blast-off eight days ago, slightly more than usual. But that figure is dwarfed by the more than 265 million hits on NASA's Mars Pathfinder mission Web site since the craft landed on July 4.

At NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, youthful scientists and engineers have raved on live television about the Mars rover and its remote-controlled perusal of rocks light-heartedly dubbed Barnacle Bill, Yogi, Casper and Scooby Doo after U.S. cartoon characters.

Meanwhile, across the country, researchers at the space agency's Marshall Space Flight Centre in Huntsville, Alabama, were trying to push the merits of complex shuttle experiments such as the "Measurement of Diffusion Coefficient by Shear Cell Method" and "Measurements of Surface Tension of Liquid and Undercooled Metallic Melts by Oscillating Drop Technique."
"The comparison is striking," one veteran space reporter said. "The Marshall guys look like they have stepped out of the Soviet Politburo."

Probably the most exciting activity aboard Columbia is a combustion research experiment that may lead to more efficient fuel consumption, Drachlis said. The astronauts are igniting blobs of flammable liquid in a specially designed chamber to understand better how flames behave in weightless conditions.
"Great balls of fire," exclaimed a NASA news release earlier this week, explaining the balls of fire were the weakest flames ever produced by man.

"We're learning that there are certain types of fuel mixtures that will burn in a space environment that couldn't burn on Earth," said Paul Ronney of the University of California in Los Angeles. "We can use this knowledge to make the next generation of spacecraft even safer."

That will be welcome news to the two Russian cosmonauts aboard Mir. Back in February they had to tackle the most serious blaze in space history when an oxygen generator burned, with a blowtorch-like flame, for nearly 15 minutes, filling the station with choking smoke.

About the time Columbia is due to end its mission, the two cosmonauts, watched by NASA colleague Mike Foale, will attempt a risky repair to recover some of the electrical power lost when a cargo craft slammed into the station last month.

In a rare ship-to-ship conversation between Foale and the shuttle crew this week, microgravity research was way down on the list of topics. "The most frustrating thing is I haven't seen a picture from Mars yet," Foale told the shuttle crew.
